title: Medicine, Tablet
paragraphs: In a classical dusky scenario enacted in the West, the Golden Apollo was being slowly swallowed by darkness of night. Consequently, the crescent moon resembled the part of a broken coconut in Lord Ganesha’s temple. In that hamlet’s temple-tank even the croaking of toads sounded distant and low.

Two men -- both middle-aged with torn, black hat, gaping khaki shirt and folded dirty dhoti-- were lurking in the bushes near the hutments. Both of them were holding shining knives. The hamlet was predominant with hutments, the sole bungalow standing apart being the only exception. The two shady characters were prowling near that bungalow.

In that hamlet, predominantly inhabited by poor masses, thieves were probably eyeing that lone bungalow. Both of them kept gesticulating to each other. At last one of them gathered courage to peer inside the house through the balcony. Nothing seemed obvious in the house dimly illuminated by a lantern. Though the eyes failed him, his ears came to his rescue.
The distinct mumbling sound a-i-u-e-o emanated from a young female. The man on the balcony opined, “Seems a pregnant woman is in travail.”

Both of them listened intently even as the grumbling stretched on. It was followed by an elderly woman’s voice, “One māttirai! One māttirai!”* The startled thieves remarked, “Seems the midwife is asking the woman to have a tablet.”
Even when the thieves were lisping, the young woman’s grumbling hit their ears: ā-ī-ū-ē-ai-ō-au. “Now two māttirai for this”. Prescribed the elderly woman.
*The word māttirai representing a unit of time in the pronunciation of sounds is homonymous with the word ‘tablet’ in English.
“Ay, the pain hasn’t subsided in one tablet; the midwife has prescribed two”, concluded the two lurking men and decided to abandon their nefarious mission in order to leave the pregnant woman alone.

“Look here, girl! The five sounds a, i, u, e and o take one māttirai each, while the seven sounds ā, ī, ū, ē, ai, ō and au are elongated taking two māttirai each. In the same manner, consonant sounds take half a māttirai each.”
“Madam! You have clearly explained the classes of letters. But I have a doubt.”
“Okay girl! What is your doubt?”
“You spoke about one māttirai, two māttirai and half a māttirai. What are they?”
“Well, the winking of eyes or the snapping of fingers forms one unit of time called māttirai. Do you understand it now?”
“I understand, madam. The units of sound (māttirai) in Tolkāppiyam have evoked sympathy among the thieves as they mistook them for the grumbling of a pregnant woman and left the place.”
“Is it so? How do you know?”
“Madam, your vision is a bit low; but I saw them in the balcony and overheard their conversation.”
“Look, girl! Tamil grammar has come to our rescue. Medicine could be consumed in tablet form but Tolkāppiyar has described the duration of sounds in terms of māttirai.
Let me elucidate further:

> The five among the thirty — > /a/, /i/, /u/, /e/ and /o/ — > Are known to be short vowels > Articulated by single phonic measures (māttirai) > So do the learned hold. > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 3)

> The seven among the thirty — > /ā/, /ī/, /ū/, /ē/, /ai/ and /au/ — > Are known to be long vowels > Taking two such phonic measures, > Thus has the authority ruled. > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 4)
> Half a phonic measure do consonants mark, > Thus goes the norm by usage set. > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 11)
> As discerning minds have seen it right, > A wink of the eyes or a snap of the fingers > Does constitute a phonic measure (māttirai). > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 7)
